meta.titre: ICT Health and Safety: matching each health problem and hazard to the right preventive measure
meta.sous_theme: Ergonomics, health problems and safety in a computer room

sections.contenu_markdown: A secretary in a busy office in Yaounde types letters and reports for most of the day. After a few months her wrists ache, her eyes are tired by the afternoon and her back hurts at the end of the week. None of this is a computer fault: it comes from the way the workstation is arranged and used. Examiners return to this theme year after year because the answers are practical and every employer must know them. A good candidate names the problem, gives its cause and proposes a measure that really prevents it.

items: A computer user often stays in the same position for hours, using a keyboard, a mouse and a screen.
Electricity can cause shocks and fires if cables, sockets or equipment are misused.
An employer is responsible for providing a safe place of work.

sections.titre: Health problems, safety hazards and ergonomic prevention
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Key terms
**Ergonomics** is the study and design of equipment, furniture and the workplace so that they fit the people who use them, in order to reduce discomfort, injury and fatigue. An **ergonomist** is the professional who advises on the layout of computers, furniture and lighting in a room.

**RSI (repetitive strain injury)** is damage to the muscles, tendons or nerves of the fingers, wrists, arms or shoulders, caused by repeating the same movement many times, usually with poor posture and too little rest. Carpal tunnel syndrome, pressure on a nerve in the wrist, is one well-known form.

### Health problems, causes and prevention
| Problem | Main causes | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| RSI | Long typing or mouse sessions; bent wrists; no rest | Regular breaks; wrist rest; keyboard at elbow height with forearms level; vary tasks |
| Eyestrain and headaches | Staring at the screen; glare and reflections; poor contrast | Anti-glare filter; adjust brightness and contrast; screen at right angles to windows; look away often; eye tests |
| Back and neck pain | Slouching; chair without support; screen too low | Adjustable chair with back support; feet flat on floor or on a footrest; screen in front, top at or just below eye level |
| Stress and fatigue | Long hours; heavy workload; noise | Scheduled breaks; varied tasks; realistic deadlines |

### Safety hazards and precautions
| Hazard | Risk | Precaution |
|---|---|---|
| Trailing cables | Tripping; damaged cable | Cable ducts or covers; tidy routing |
| Too many devices on one socket | Overheating and fire | Spread the load; respect the rating of sockets and leads |
| Drinks near equipment | Electric shock; damaged equipment | No food or drink in the room |
| Faulty equipment | Electric shock | Switch off, report it, repair by a qualified technician |
| Fire | Injury; loss of equipment | Smoke detectors; CO2 or dry-powder extinguisher, never water on electrical equipment; clear exits |
| Poor ventilation | Overheating of machines and people | Good ventilation, fans or air conditioning |

### Answering well
A mark is normally given for a **named problem** and a mark for a **matching measure**. A measure must act on the cause: a wrist rest helps RSI but does nothing for eyestrain.

variantes.nom: State or list the health problems
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command word is state, name or list.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give the problem in a few words and add its cause in the same line, for example: "RSI, caused by repeated typing with bent wrists". Do not write a paragraph: one precise line earns the mark.

variantes.nom: Measures taken by the employer and by the user
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks how an organisation or a worker can prevent a problem.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Employer**: provide adjustable chairs, footrests, anti-glare screens and good lighting; organise a risk assessment; allow breaks; train staff in posture; arrange eye tests. **User**: sit correctly, take breaks, adjust the screen and chair, keep the area tidy and report faults. Say who acts and what they do.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks how equipment can be designed to reduce health problems.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Adjustable-height and tilting monitors; keyboards shaped or placed to keep the wrists straight; wrist and palm rests; adjustable chairs with lumbar support; footrests; document holders that stop the neck twisting; anti-glare coatings. Each feature links to one problem.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A data-entry clerk in a transport company in Douala types waybills for six hours a day. She reports three complaints: a tingling pain in her right wrist, headaches that begin in the afternoon, and a sore lower back. Her screen stands on a low table in front of a large window, and she sits on a plastic stool.

(a) Name the likely health problem behind each complaint and its cause.

(b) Recommend one precise measure for each complaint.

(c) Name the professional who should be asked to redesign the workstation.

etapes.action: Read the command words and count the marks.
etapes.justification: Three complaints are given, and (a) and (b) each ask for something per complaint, so the answer needs six items plus one name.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Plan: three lines for (a) (problem and cause), three lines for (b) (measure), one line for (c).

etapes.action: Match the wrist complaint to its problem.
etapes.justification: A pain caused by long repeated typing is the definition of a repetitive strain injury.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Wrist: **RSI**, caused by many hours of repeated typing and mouse use without enough rest. Measure: regular short breaks and a wrist rest, with the keyboard at elbow height.

etapes.action: Match the headaches to their problem, using the clue of the window.
etapes.justification: Afternoon headaches with a screen placed in front of a window point to glare and eyestrain, not to a posture problem.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Headaches: **eyestrain**, caused by glare and reflections and by staring at the screen for long periods. Measure: turn the screen at right angles to the window (or use blinds) and fit an anti-glare filter.

etapes.action: Match the back pain to its problem, using the clue of the stool.
etapes.justification: A seat without back support and a screen that is too low make the user slouch and bend the neck.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Lower back: **back and neck strain** from poor posture. Measure: replace the stool with an adjustable chair with back support and raise the screen so that its top is at or just below eye level.

etapes.action: Answer part (c) with the exact title.
etapes.justification: The professional who advises on the arrangement of computers, furniture and lighting is the specialist in ergonomics.

sections.conclusion_markdown:
(a) Wrist: RSI (repeated typing). Headaches: eyestrain (glare, long screen use). Lower back: back strain (poor posture, no support).

(b) Wrist: regular breaks and a wrist rest. Headaches: screen at right angles to the window and an anti-glare filter. Back: adjustable chair with back support and a correctly raised screen.

(c) An ergonomist.

items.erreur_markdown: "RSI is caused by radiation coming from the screen."
items.pourquoi_faux: RSI is an injury of muscles, tendons and nerves from repeated movements and poor posture. The screen is linked to eyestrain, not to RSI.
items.correction_markdown: "RSI is caused by repeating the same movement, such as typing, for long periods without rest."

items.erreur_markdown: "Ergonomics is the study of computer keyboards."
items.pourquoi_faux: Keyboards are only one example. Ergonomics covers the design of all equipment, furniture and the workplace so that they fit the user.
items.correction_markdown: "Ergonomics is the design of equipment and the working environment to fit the user and to reduce health problems."

items.erreur_markdown: "To avoid health problems, the worker should be careful and use the computer less."
items.pourquoi_faux: The answer is vague. It names no action that acts on a cause, so it earns no mark.
items.correction_markdown: Name a precise measure: "take a five-minute break every hour", "fit an anti-glare filter", "use an adjustable chair with back support".

items.pourquoi_faux: A measure must act on the cause of the problem named. A wrist rest supports the wrists; eyestrain comes from glare and long screen use.
items.correction_markdown: Match them: wrist rest for RSI; anti-glare filter and regular rests from the screen for eyestrain.

items.erreur_markdown: "If a computer catches fire, pour water on it."
items.pourquoi_faux: Water conducts electricity, so it can cause electric shock to the person and does not safely put out an electrical fire.
items.correction_markdown: Switch off the power if it is safe to do so, and use a CO2 or dry-powder extinguisher. Raise the alarm and leave by the fire exit.

items.enonce_markdown:
For each situation, name the problem or hazard and give one measure that prevents it.

(a) A typist has a stiff neck at the end of each day because her screen is placed on the floor beside the desk.

(b) An accountant has tingling fingers after typing figures for several hours without stopping.

(c) A visitor trips over a cable that crosses the office floor.

(d) A technician uses a metal-handled screwdriver inside a computer that is still switched on at the wall.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Neck and back strain** from a poorly placed screen. Measure: place the screen directly in front, with its top at or just below eye level.

(b) **RSI**. Measure: take regular breaks and keep the wrists straight, with the keyboard at elbow height.

(c) **Trailing cable (tripping hazard)**. Measure: route the cable along the wall or through a cable duct or cover.

(d) **Electric shock**. Measure: switch off and unplug the computer before opening it; repairs only by a qualified person.

items.enonce_markdown:
An office manager adopts this rule for clerks who key in data all morning: work for 50 minutes, then take a break of 10 minutes, and repeat. A clerk starts at 08:00 and finishes at 13:00, beginning with a keying period.

(a) How many complete cycles of 50 minutes of work and 10 minutes of break does she complete?

(b) How much time does she spend keying, in hours and minutes? What percentage of her shift is that, to one decimal place?

(c) State the health problem this rule mainly reduces, and one other measure at the workstation that helps the same problem.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The shift lasts 300 minutes and each cycle lasts 60 minutes: 300 ÷ 60 = **5 cycles**.

(b) Keying time = 5 × 50 = 250 minutes = **4 h 10 min**. Percentage = 250 ÷ 300 × 100 = **83.3%** of the shift (the other 50 minutes are breaks).

(c) Regular breaks mainly reduce **RSI** (and rest the eyes). Another measure for RSI is a wrist rest, or placing the keyboard at elbow height so that the wrists stay straight.

items.enonce_markdown:
A computer room has six computers of 150 W each and one printer of 600 W, all plugged into a single extension lead rated at 10 A. Assume a supply of 220 V and use current = power ÷ voltage.

(a) Calculate the current taken by one computer, to two decimal places.

(b) Calculate the total current taken by the six computers and the printer, and say whether the lead is overloaded.

(c) What is the greatest total power that the lead can carry?

(d) A 1000 W heater is then plugged into the same lead. Calculate the new current and explain the danger. Give two safe changes.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) I = P ÷ U = 150 ÷ 220 = **0.68 A**.

(b) Total power = 6 × 150 + 600 = 1500 W. I = 1500 ÷ 220 = **6.82 A**. This is below 10 A, so the lead is **not overloaded**.

(c) P = I × U = 10 × 220 = **2200 W**.

(d) New total = 1500 + 1000 = 2500 W, so I = 2500 ÷ 220 = **11.36 A**, which is above 10 A. The lead is overloaded: it overheats, the insulation can melt and a fire can start. Safe changes: do not connect the heater to this lead (use a separate socket or circuit), and spread the load over several sockets with correctly rated leads.

items_markdown: Ergonomics is the design of equipment and the workplace to fit the user; the specialist who advises on it is an ergonomist.
RSI comes from repeated movements and poor posture; eyestrain comes from glare and long screen use; back and neck pain comes from poor posture and unsuitable furniture.
A good answer pairs each named problem with a measure that acts on its cause: breaks and wrist rest for RSI, anti-glare filter for eyes, adjustable chair for the back.
Safety hazards are different from health problems: trailing cables, overloaded sockets, spilled drinks, faulty equipment, fire and poor ventilation each have their own precaution.
Never use water on an electrical fire. Switch off the power if it is safe, use a CO2 or dry-powder extinguisher and leave by the fire exit.
Both the employer (equipment, training, breaks) and the user (posture, breaks, reporting faults) have responsibilities.
